title: Puzzles
strapline: Turn it, try it, nearly... yes! Puzzles teach children that stuck is just a stop on the way to done.
intent: Children develop shape and space sense — rotating, flipping and fitting pieces, judging what will and won't go.
Children learn problem-solving strategies: edges first, match the colours, look at the picture, try another way.
Children build persistence with a task that has a real, visible finish — the puzzle is done or it isn't.
Children refine the precise finger control needed to place, nudge and press a piece home.
Children learn to work on a shared problem with a friend — dividing the pieces, helping without taking over.
implementation: Grade the range openly: chunky knobbed insets, then lift-outs, then jigsaws from 4 to 24+ pieces — children should always see a next step up.
Resist the hovering hand. Offer strategy, not pieces: 'try turning it', 'look for the corner bits', 'what colour is next to that bit in the picture?'
Name the almost: 'so close — it's the right shape, just upside down' keeps a child in the game where 'no' ends it.
Sit with a puzzle yourself sometimes and think aloud, including getting stuck and trying again.
Keep puzzles complete and respected — check pieces at tidy-up, retire anything with gaps; an unfinishable puzzle teaches exactly the wrong lesson.
Offer big floor puzzles for pairs and trios, and quietly scaffold the sharing: 'you two have half the pieces each'.
Photograph the completed puzzle with its finisher — done deserves recording.
key_questions: Where do you think this piece might go?
What could you try if it doesn't fit?
Which bit will you do first — how did you choose?
What's the picture telling you about where this goes?
You were stuck a minute ago — what changed?

impact.text: Children fit shapes into spaces, complete inset puzzles and move themselves on to harder boards.
Children match pieces by noticing what's the same and different — colour, pattern, shape of the edge.
Children use position words as they work — 'it goes next to the tractor, in the corner, behind the tree'.
Children place and press pieces with precise, patient finger control.
Children stay with a tricky puzzle to the last piece and beam 'I did it!' rather than waiting to be rescued.
Children tackle a floor puzzle together, sharing pieces, taking turns and helping a friend find a fit.
Children talk through their strategy — 'I'm finding all the edge ones first' — showing they have a plan.

enhancements: Photo puzzles of the children themselves and the nursery garden — cut-up laminated photos are the most fought-over puzzles in the room.
A 'puzzle of the week' table where one ambitious jigsaw stays out mid-build, ready to return to — done over days, not minutes.
Homemade story puzzles: scenes from a core book to rebuild and retell in order.
Wooden number and name insets so fitting shapes doubles as meeting numerals and letters.
A sand timer for the child who wants to race themselves — never each other — on a favourite board.
Cooperative floor maps of the local streets: find the nursery, the park, the shops as you build.
A 'stuck box' ritual — a puzzle that beat you today can wait safely in the box for tomorrow's try.

playing_exploring: Children choose their own level of challenge and climb the range at their own pace.
Familiar puzzles get revisited for the pleasure of mastery — that's practice, freely chosen.
active_learning: Puzzles are persistence made visible: every piece placed is progress you can see.
The finished picture is a built-in goal children hold in mind all the way through.
creating_thinking: Children develop and swap real strategies — edges first, sort by colour, check the picture.
Trying a piece, failing, rotating and trying again is hypothesis-testing in miniature.
